Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes

10 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Is a nation the same thing as a state, and why do the two so rarely line up?
  2. Mission 2Why did sixteen African countries join the United Nations in a single year?
  3. Mission 3Why did Canada and Denmark spend decades planting flags on a tiny island where nobody lives?
  4. Mission 4Why are so many of Africa's borders ruler-straight lines?
  5. Mission 5Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognize their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?
  6. Mission 6Can the same voters elect different winners just by moving the lines on a map?
  7. Mission 7Why can the speed limit change the moment you drive from one US state into the next?
  8. Mission 8Why do some countries split apart, while others hold together by handing power to their regions?
  9. Mission 9From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?
  10. Mission 10In 2023 Somalia topped the Fragile States Index. What pulls a country apart, and what holds one together?

Every fact and figure is sourced: see the Sources list under the lesson.

Mission 1

Mission 1: Is a nation the same thing as a state, and why do the two so rarely line up?

Make a guess: Is a nation the same thing as a state, and why do the two so rarely line up?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • PSO-4.A for world political maps, define types of political entities and identify contemporary examples
  • PSO-4.A.1 independent states are the primary building blocks of the world political map
  • PSO-4.A.2 types of political entities include nations, nation-states, stateless nations, multinational states, multistate nations, and autonomous and semiautonomous regions such as Native American reservations
Mission 1

The state

  • A state (an independent country) needs, by the 1933 Montevideo Convention: "a permanent population", "a defined territory", "government" and the "capacity to enter into relations with the other states".
  • States hold sovereignty: the final authority over their territory.
  • States are the building blocks of the world political map. The UN has 193 member states.
Mission 1

The nation

  • A nation is a people: a group who share a culture, history and often a language, and see themselves as one community.
  • A nation is about identity; a state is about territory and government.
  • Many nations want their own state, or at least to govern themselves (self-determination).
Quick check
?Which of these is a state rather than a nation?
Mission 1

The nation-state

  • A nation-state: one nation fills one state, and the state's borders match the nation's homeland.
  • It is an ideal: almost every state includes minorities, and many nations live in more than one state.
  • States often described as close to nation-states include Japan and Iceland.
Mission 1

Multinational states

  • A multinational state contains two or more nations.
  • Example: the United Kingdom: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
  • In 2014 people in Scotland voted in a referendum "to remain in the United Kingdom": a nation inside a larger state.
Mission 1

Multistate nations and stateless nations

  • A multistate nation: one nation spread across two or more states. Example: Koreans, in North Korea and South Korea; both states joined the UN on September 17, 1991.
  • A stateless nation: a nation without a state of its own. Example: the Kurds, who live mainly in parts of Turkey, Iran, Iraq, Syria and Armenia; they "have never achieved nation-state status in the modern era".
  • The Kurds are both stateless and multistate.
Quick check
?Why are the Kurds called a stateless nation?
Mission 1

Autonomous and semiautonomous regions

  • An autonomous or semiautonomous region governs some of its own affairs but stays part of a larger state.
  • Native American reservations: about 326 land areas are administered as federal Indian reservations; they are "generally exempt from state jurisdiction".
  • Kurdistan Region, Iraq: recognized by Iraq's 2005 constitution as a federal region with its own authorities.
  • Hong Kong: a Special Administrative Region with "a high degree of autonomy", inside China.
Mission 1

Reservations up close

  • About 56.2 million acres are held in trust by the United States for tribes and individuals.
  • The largest reservation is the Navajo Nation: 16 million acres across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah.
  • There are 575 federally recognized tribes; not every tribe has a reservation.
  • Tribes have powers of self-government, but within the United States: semiautonomous, not independent.
Quick check
?The Navajo Nation Reservation covers 16 million acres; all US Indian trust land covers 56.2 million acres. About what share of the trust land is the Navajo reservation?
Mission 1

Reading the political map

  • The map shows states; nations and autonomous regions are often invisible on it.
  • Mismatches between nations and states help explain independence movements, boundary disputes and devolution (later on this page).
  • AP move: name the entity type, then give a contemporary example and its feature.
Mission check

?An invented people, the Varans, share a language and history. Their homeland is split between two neighboring states, and they have no independent state. In one of those states they elect a regional parliament that runs schools and policing. Which terms fit?

States (sovereign territories) are the building blocks of the political map; nations (peoples) rarely fit them exactly, giving nation-states, multinational states, multistate nations, stateless nations and autonomous regions such as Native American reservations.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Why did sixteen African countries join the United Nations in a single year?

Make a guess: Why did sixteen African countries join the United Nations in a single year?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • PSO-4.B explain the processes that have shaped contemporary political geography
  • PSO-4.B.1 sovereignty, nation-states and self-determination shape the contemporary world
  • PSO-4.B.2 colonialism, imperialism, independence movements and devolution along national lines have influenced contemporary political boundaries
Mission 2

Sovereignty

  • Sovereignty: a state's supreme authority over its own territory, free from outside control.
  • The UN "is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its Members".
  • The UN may not intervene "in matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state".
Mission 2

Nation-state and self-determination

  • Nation: a people with a shared culture and identity. State: a sovereign territory with a government.
  • Nation-state: where the borders of one nation and one state largely match.
  • Self-determination: the idea that a people may choose its own government. The UN Charter names "the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples".
Quick check
?A group with its own language and history argues it should be free to set up its own government. Which principle is it using?
Mission 2

Imperialism drew the lines

  • At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), "the major European nations met to decide all questions connected with the Congo River basin".
  • European powers divided much of Africa among themselves; most borders were drawn without the people who lived there.
  • In 1945, "some 750 million people", "nearly a third of the world's population", lived in territories dependent on colonial powers.
Mission 2

Independence movements

  • Colonized peoples organized to demand self-rule.
  • In 1960 the UN General Assembly adopted its Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples.
  • In 1960 alone, UN membership rose from 82 to 99: 17 new members, 16 of them African (counted from the UN list).
  • "Since the creation of the United Nations, 80 former colonies have gained their independence"; 17 Non-Self-Governing Territories remain.
Mission 2

India 1947: one colony, two states

  • From August 15, 1947, "two independent Dominions shall be set up in India", named India and Pakistan.
  • A colonial power's exit created a new international boundary that had not existed before.
Mission 2

Colonial lines stayed

  • Most new African states kept the borders drawn by colonial powers.
  • The International Court of Justice describes "the principle of the intangibility of frontiers inherited from colonization".
  • Its aim: "to secure respect for the territorial boundaries which existed at the time when independence was achieved".
  • Result: some states hold several nations; some nations are split across states.
Quick check
?Why do many of Africa's international borders today match lines drawn in the colonial era?
Mission 2

Devolution along national lines

  • Devolution: a state transfers power to regions; sometimes regions go on to break away.
  • Soviet Union: "the Baltic States and the Caucasus demanded independence from Moscow"; in December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved. The Baltic States plus 12 other republics became independent states: 15 in all (our calculation).
  • United Kingdom: the Scotland Act 1998: "There shall be a Scottish Parliament." Scotland gained powers but stayed in the UK.
Mission 2

South Sudan: the newest state

  • The 2005 peace agreement "granted southern Sudan semiautonomous status".
  • A January 2011 referendum showed "the south's overwhelming preference to secede".
  • "The country of South Sudan declared independence on July 9, 2011." It became the UN's 193rd member.
Quick check
?Which change is devolution but not independence?
Mission check

?In a hypothetical state, the people of one northern region speak their own language. The national government gives the region its own parliament. Twenty years later, the region votes to leave and is recognized as a new state. Which sequence of processes best describes this?

Colonialism drew many borders; independence movements turned colonies into sovereign states, often keeping colonial lines. Devolution along national lines can shift power within a state or, as in the Soviet Union and South Sudan, create new states.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Why did Canada and Denmark spend decades planting flags on a tiny island where nobody lives?

Make a guess: Why did Canada and Denmark spend decades planting flags on a tiny island where nobody lives?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • PSO-4.C describe the concepts of political power and territoriality as used by geographers
  • PSO-4.C.1 political power is expressed geographically as control over people, land and resources, as illustrated by neocolonialism, shatterbelts and choke points
  • PSO-4.C.2 territoriality is the connection of people, their culture and their economic systems to the land
Mission 3

Political power on the map

  • Political power is expressed geographically as control over:
    • people (who lives under which laws),
    • land (who owns and rules territory),
    • resources (oil, water, sea routes, fish).
  • This mission: territoriality, then three expressions of power: neocolonialism, shatterbelts, choke points.
Mission 3

Territoriality

  • Territoriality: the connection of people, their culture and their economic systems to the land.
  • It shows in behavior: naming, mapping, marking, guarding and defending a space.
  • Scales: a gang's turf, a farm's fence, a nation's border.
Mission 3

Hans Island: the flags

  • A 1.3 km², uninhabited island lying "midway" between Canada and Greenland (part of the Kingdom of Denmark).
  • A 1973 treaty on the sea border "deliberately left the border undefined" through the island.
  • For decades both countries' forces occasionally landed, raised their flags and left a bottle of whisky or aquavit: the "Whisky War".
Mission 3

Hans Island: the settlement

  • On June 14, 2022, Canada and Denmark, together with Greenland, signed an agreement resolving the boundary.
  • The island is "divided along a natural ridge", roughly 60% to Denmark (Greenland) and the rest to Canada.
  • The deal keeps "freedom of movement on the entirety of the island"; Inuit of Nunavut and Greenland were consulted.
  • Both states tied their nation to a rock nobody lives on: that is territoriality.
Quick check
?Which action is the clearest example of territoriality?
Mission 3

Neocolonialism

  • Neocolonialism: control of a formally independent country by outside powers through economic means rather than direct rule.
  • Ghana's first president, Kwame Nkrumah, wrote in 1965 that such a state is "in theory, independent", but "its economic system and thus its political policy is directed from outside".
  • He argued control is "more often" exercised "through economic or monetary means".
Mission 3

Neocolonialism: what the data show

  • UNCTAD counts a country as commodity-dependent when raw materials make up more than 60% of its merchandise exports.
  • In 2019–21, 95 of 142 developing countries were commodity-dependent; in Africa, 45 of 53.
  • Critics of neocolonialism see this dependence on selling raw materials to richer economies as a channel of outside control. Others explain it by geology, history and policy. The data show the dependence; the cause is debated.
Mission 3

Shatterbelts

  • Shatterbelt: a region divided internally and caught between rival outside powers, so it is often unstable.
  • Example: the Middle East in the Cold War.
    • After the 1956 Suez Crisis, Soviet influence grew in Egypt and Syria.
    • In January 1957 the USA answered with the Eisenhower Doctrine: US aid and forces for states facing "armed aggression from any nation controlled by international communism".
    • Each superpower sought allies among the region's divided states.
Quick check
?A region has many small states with internal divisions, and two rival world powers compete for influence over them. What is this region best called?
Mission 3

Choke points

  • Choke point: a narrow passage, such as a strait or canal, that a large share of shipping must use.
  • Strait of Hormuz, 2024: oil flow averaged 20 million barrels a day, about 20% of world petroleum liquids consumption.
  • 84% of the crude oil and condensate passing through went to Asian markets.
  • Whoever can block or protect a choke point holds power over others' resources.
Mission 3

When choke points close

  • Red Sea: attacks on ships led most shipping lines to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope. By June 2024, Suez Canal transits were down 70%.
  • Hormuz: conflict in Iran from February 28, 2026 brought "the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz", lowering oil output in the region.
  • Control of a narrow passage reaches economies far away.
Mission check

?For generations, families in an imaginary fishing village have fished the same bay; their festivals and place names come from it. When their own national government plans to lease the bay to a large fish farm, villagers put up signs, patrol the water and protest. Which concept best explains the villagers' response?

The flags on Hans Island and the villagers' patrols are both territoriality: people tie their nation, culture or living to land, then mark and defend it. Political power is control over people, land and resources, seen also in neocolonialism, shatterbelts and choke points.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Why are so many of Africa's borders ruler-straight lines?

Make a guess: Why are so many of Africa's borders ruler-straight lines?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • IMP-4.A define types of political boundaries
  • IMP-4.A.1 relict, superimposed, subsequent, antecedent, geometric, consequent
  • IMP-4.B explain the nature and function of international and internal boundaries
  • IMP-4.B.1 boundaries are defined, delimited, demarcated and administered to limit sovereignty, but often contested
  • IMP-4.B.2 boundaries often follow cultural, national or economic divisions; some come from DMZs or policy, e.g. the Berlin Conference
Mission 4

What a boundary does

  • A boundary marks the limit of a state's sovereignty: where its laws and control stop.
  • International boundaries separate countries. Internal boundaries separate states, provinces or districts inside one country.
  • Boundaries can also follow divisions in culture (language, religion), nationality or economy.
Mission 4

How a boundary is made

1. Defined: written in words in a treaty or legal document. 2. Delimited: drawn on a map. 3. Demarcated: marked on the ground (posts, pillars, fences, walls). 4. Administered: the state controls it: who and what can cross, and how.

Mission 4

One boundary, four steps

  • Defined: the US–UK Convention of 1818 said the boundary would run "along" the 49th parallel from Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains; an 1846 treaty extended it west.
  • Delimited: commissions surveyed and mapped the line west of the Rockies (from 1858) and west of Lake of the Woods (from 1872); a 1908 treaty called for accurate modern charts.
  • Demarcated: land sections were "marked by monuments, mounds or rock cairns".
  • Administered: a joint US–Canada commission maintains the line, and today it watches any construction within 3 meters (10 feet) of it.
Mission 4

Contested: a line on paper only

  • After a war, Eritrea and Ethiopia signed the Algiers Agreement (December 12, 2000), which set up a Boundary Commission.
  • The Commission delimited the boundary in a unanimous decision of April 13, 2002.
  • Demarcation stalled: only part of the eastern sector was marked, in 2003.
  • In 2007 the Commission fixed the pillar points on paper, using satellite images and terrain models, and declared them binding.
  • So a boundary can be legally fixed but still unmarked, and contested, on the ground.
Quick check
?Surveyors from two countries place concrete pillars every few miles along a boundary their governments agreed on in a treaty. Which step is this?
Mission 4

Types by when they were drawn

  • Antecedent: drawn before many people settled the area.
  • Subsequent: drawn after settlement, as the cultural landscape took shape.
  • Consequent: a subsequent boundary drawn to match cultural divisions, such as language or religion. Example: Belgium's internal language boundary separates Dutch-speaking Flanders from French-speaking Wallonia.
  • Superimposed: forced on an area by an outside power, ignoring the cultures already there.
Mission 4

Geometric and relict

  • Geometric: a straight line, often a line of latitude or longitude. Example: the 49th parallel between the USA and Canada.
  • Relict: a boundary that no longer functions, but can still be seen in the landscape.
  • Example: the Berlin Wall surrounded West Berlin from August 13, 1961, to November 9, 1989. The border around West Berlin was 155 kilometers long. "Numerous remnants" are still visible today.
Quick check
?Parts of the Berlin Wall still stand in Berlin, but people walk freely past them. What type of boundary are they now?
Mission 4

Boundaries made by policy: the Berlin Conference

  • From November 15, 1884, to February 26, 1885, major European powers met in Berlin to decide questions about the Congo River basin in Central Africa.
  • The talks were held in Europe, among European governments.
  • In the decades that followed, European powers claimed most of Africa. Many lines were drawn on maps in Europe, often straight, cutting across existing ethnic and cultural regions.
  • So many African borders are superimposed and geometric at the same time.
Mission 4

Boundaries made by ceasefires: DMZs

  • A demilitarized zone (DMZ): a strip where armed forces agree not to station troops or weapons.
  • Example: the DMZ between North Korea and South Korea, set by the armistice that halted the Korean War. It still divides the peninsula today.
  • A DMZ boundary comes from a military agreement, not from culture or physical features.
Quick check
?A boundary was drawn by an empire to split two colonies. It cuts straight through the lands of one language group. Which pair of types fits best?
Mission check

?In a desert region, two herding peoples have used the same wells for centuries. A distant empire draws a border along a line of longitude to divide the region between two of its colonies. Why is this border straight, and what problem may follow?

Many of Africa's straight borders were drawn by outside powers on maps, after the Berlin Conference. They are superimposed and geometric, and many cut across peoples who lived there long before.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognize their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?

Make a guess: Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognize their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • IMP-4.B explain the nature and function of international and internal boundaries
  • IMP-4.B.3 land and maritime boundaries and agreements shape identity, encourage or discourage interaction, and spark resource disputes
  • IMP-4.B.4 UNCLOS defines rights in international waters, territorial seas and exclusive economic zones
Mission 5

Boundaries at sea

  • On land, boundaries mark the limits of a state's sovereignty. At sea, a treaty sets the limits.
  • The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) was adopted in 1982 and entered into force in 1994. It has 172 parties.
  • Distances are measured in nautical miles (nm) from the baseline, usually the low-water line along the coast.
Mission 5

Territorial sea and contiguous zone

  • Territorial sea: up to 12 nm from the baseline. The state's sovereignty covers the water, the air space above, and the seabed below.
  • Ships of all states, "whether coastal or land-locked", keep a right of innocent passage through it.
  • Contiguous zone: up to 24 nm, for customs, tax, immigration and health controls.
Mission 5

Exclusive economic zone (EEZ)

  • EEZ: up to 200 nm from the baseline.
  • The coastal state has sovereign rights over natural resources, "whether living or non-living": fish, oil, gas, minerals.
  • Other states keep "freedoms … of navigation and overflight" and can lay submarine cables and pipelines.
  • So the EEZ is about resources, not full sovereignty.
Mission 5

International waters

  • Beyond the EEZs lie the high seas: international waters. "The high seas are open to all States, whether coastal or land-locked".
  • Freedoms there include navigation, overflight, fishing (under conditions), scientific research and laying cables.
  • "No State may validly purport to subject any part of the high seas to its sovereignty".
  • The seabed beyond national limits is the Area, "the common heritage of mankind", managed by the International Seabed Authority (ISA).
Quick check
?A fishing boat from Country X sails 50 nm off the coast of Country Y. Which statement is correct?
Mission 5

When zones overlap

  • Where coasts are less than 400 nm apart, two 200-nm EEZs overlap.
  • Territorial seas: unless the states agree otherwise, neither may go beyond the median line, halfway between their coasts.
  • EEZs: the boundary is set "by agreement on the basis of international law … in order to achieve an equitable solution".
  • The AP course uses the median-line principle for overlapping EEZs.
Mission 5

An agreement that encouraged interaction

  • Norway and Russia disputed about 175,000 km² of the Barents Sea for some 40 years.
  • Their 2010 treaty divided the area into "two parts of approximately the same size". It entered into force on July 7, 2011.
  • It kept "close Norwegian–Russian cooperation on fisheries" and set rules for cooperating on any oil or gas deposit that crosses the line.
  • A settled boundary made joint use of resources easier, not harder.
Mission 5

A dispute over resources: the South China Sea

  • The Philippines took China to an arbitration tribunal set up under UNCLOS.
  • On July 12, 2016, the tribunal found "no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources" inside its "nine-dash line".
  • It found that China had violated the Philippines' rights in its EEZ, including by interfering with Philippine fishing and petroleum exploration.
  • China's position: it did not accept or take part in the arbitration, and stated that the tribunal "does not have jurisdiction".
Mission 5

The Arctic seabed

  • A state's continental shelf can extend beyond 200 nm where its continental margin does. UNCLOS caps it at 350 nm or at 100 nm beyond the 2,500 m depth line.
  • Claims beyond 200 nm go to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS): Russia (2001; revised 2015), Denmark for Greenland (2014), Canada (2019).
  • Denmark's submission says Canada's limits "would overlap" Greenland's; the Lomonosov Ridge is central to the claims.
  • In 2008 the five Arctic Ocean coastal states committed to "orderly settlement of any possible overlapping claims". The CLCS reviews the science; the states settle the boundaries.
Mission 5

Boundaries, identity and interaction

  • Land, encouraging interaction: the Schengen area's 29 countries have abolished checks at their internal borders, giving free movement to "more than 450 million EU citizens".
  • Sea, regional identity: in 2021 Pacific Islands Forum leaders declared together that their maritime zones "shall continue to apply, without reduction", even if rising seas change their coastlines.
  • They called climate change and sea-level rise the "defining issue" that imperils "the livelihoods and wellbeing of our peoples": a shared regional position built on ocean boundaries.
  • Discouraging interaction: unresolved claims, as in the South China Sea, can bring confrontation over fishing and drilling.
Quick check
?Which example best shows a maritime agreement encouraging international interaction?
Mission check

?A small island state finds metal-rich nodules on the seabed 150 nm from its coast. More nodules lie on the deep seabed 900 nm from any coast. Who has rights to each?

Under UNCLOS, coastal states have resource rights to 200 nm (and over their continental shelf, sometimes beyond). The deep seabed beyond that is the Area, a "common heritage" managed by the ISA. In the Arctic, overlapping shelf claims go to the CLCS for the science, and to negotiation for the boundaries.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Can the same voters elect different winners just by moving the lines on a map?

Make a guess: Can the same voters elect different winners just by moving the lines on a map?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • IMP-4.B explain the nature and function of international and internal boundaries (internal boundaries here)
  • IMP-4.B.5 voting districts, redistricting and gerrymandering affect election results at various scales
Mission 6

Voting districts

  • A voting district: an area whose voters elect a representative.
  • The US House has 435 seats, shared among the 50 states by population.
  • This apportionment happens "every 10 years based on population counts from the decennial census".
  • Each state then splits its seats into districts with nearly equal populations.
Mission 6

Redistricting

  • Redistricting: redrawing district lines, usually after each census.
  • After the 2020 Census, Texas gained two seats; seven states lost one each. Those states had to draw new maps.
  • Districts exist at many scales: US House seats, state legislatures, city councils, school boards.
  • Whoever draws the lines can shape the results.
Mission 6

Gerrymandering

  • Gerrymandering: drawing district lines to give one party or group an advantage.
  • The name dates from 1812: Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry approved districts drawn to help his party, and a newspaper said one district looked like a salamander.
  • Gerrymandered districts often have odd, stretched shapes, though shape alone does not prove it.
Mission 6

Two tools: packing and cracking

  • Packing: putting as many of a party's supporters as possible into a few districts. They win those by huge margins, "wasting" many votes.
  • Cracking: splitting a party's supporters across many districts, "so that they fall short of a majority in each".
  • Both reduce the number of seats a group wins compared with its share of votes.
Quick check
?A party's supporters live together in one city. Mapmakers divide the city into five slices, each joined to a large rural area where the other party is strong. The party now loses all five districts. Which tool is this?
Mission 6

Same voters, three maps

A hypothetical state: 50 voters, 30 Purple (60%) and 20 Orange (40%), 5 districts of 10 voters each.

  • Map 1: every district has 6 Purple, 4 Orange → Purple wins 5–0 (Orange cracked).
  • Map 2: three districts of 8 Purple, 2 Orange; two of 3 Purple, 7 Orange → Purple 3, Orange 2.
  • Map 3: three districts of 4 Purple, 6 Orange; two of 9 Purple, 1 Orange → Orange wins 3–2 (Purple packed).
  • Same votes. Different winners.
Quick check
?A hypothetical state has 60 Blue and 40 Green voters in 5 districts of 20. Mapmakers draw two districts of 20 Blue each. The other three districts get the remaining 20 Blue and 40 Green: 7 Blue + 13 Green, 7 Blue + 13 Green, 6 Blue + 14 Green. How many seats does Green win?
Mission 6

The courts and the scale of the lines

  • Equal populations: in Wesberry v. Sanders (1964), the Supreme Court held that "one man's vote in a congressional election is to be worth as much as another's".
  • City scale: in Gomillion v. Lightfoot (1960), the Court found a constitutional claim against an "uncouth twenty-eight sided" city boundary that excluded Black voters from city elections.
  • Partisan gerrymandering: in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Court held that such claims "present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts".
Mission 6

Who draws the lines?

  • After Rucho, the main checks on partisan gerrymanders are state courts, laws and constitutions.
  • Example: in 2015, Florida's Supreme Court struck down the state's congressional map under its "Fair Districts" amendment.
  • In 2018, voters in Colorado and Michigan approved independent commissions to draw maps.
  • So the rules on drawing lines themselves vary from state to state.
Quick check
?After 2019, which body could most directly stop a partisan gerrymander of a state's congressional map?
Mission check

?A city has 100,000 voters in 4 council districts of 25,000 voters each. Party M wins 52% of the votes citywide. Which set of district results shows a map on which Party M wins only one seat?

All four maps average 52% for Party M, yet they give it 4, 3, 2 or 1 seats. Where the lines go, from Congress down to a city council, can change who wins.

Mission 7

Mission 7: Why can the speed limit change the moment you drive from one US state into the next?

Make a guess: Why can the speed limit change the moment you drive from one US state into the next?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • IMP-4.C define federal and unitary states
  • IMP-4.C.1 forms of governance include unitary and federal states
  • IMP-4.D explain how federal and unitary states affect spatial organization
  • IMP-4.D.1 unitary states are more top-down and centralized; federal states have more locally based, dispersed power centers
Mission 7

Who holds the power?

  • A unitary state: power is held by the central (national) government. Regions carry out what the center decides.
  • A federal state: power is shared between a national government and regional governments (states, provinces). Each level has powers the other cannot take away on its own.
  • Unitary = top-down, centralized. Federal = dispersed power centers.
Mission 7

Federal: the United States

  • The Tenth Amendment: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people."
  • So all 50 states have their own governments that make laws on many topics.
  • That is why many laws, such as speed limits, change at state lines.
Mission 7

Federal: Germany

  • Germany's Basic Law calls the country "a democratic and social federal state".
  • Its states are called Länder. "The Länder shall have the right to legislate insofar as this Basic Law does not confer legislative power on the Federation."
  • School education is one of the "legislative powers exclusive to the Länder".
Mission 7

Unitary: France

  • France's Constitution: "France shall be an indivisible... Republic."
  • Its regions and departments are local governments, but in each one a State representative is "responsible for national interests, administrative supervision and compliance with the law".
  • Prefects (the State's representatives) are "appointed in the Council of Ministers", which is the national government.
  • Power runs from Paris outward.
Quick check
?Which description fits a federal state?
Mission 7

How the map looks: federal

  • Many power centers: each state or Land has its own capital, legislature and laws.
  • Laws form a patchwork on the map. Example: maximum speed limits on rural interstates range from 60 mph in Hawaii to 85 mph on specified Texas roads.
  • Policies can differ from region to region, so people and businesses may move to the state whose laws suit them.
Mission 7

How the map looks: unitary

  • One dominant power center: the capital.
  • Laws and services tend to be uniform across the country.
  • Regions are run by officials who answer to the center, such as French prefects.
  • Big decisions about roads, schools and budgets are made in the capital.
Quick check
?A map shows that school-leaving rules differ from one region of a country to the next. What does this most likely suggest?
Mission 7

In between: devolution

  • A unitary state can devolve (hand down) some powers to regions.
  • Example: the UK's Scotland Act 1998: "There shall be a Scottish Parliament."
  • But the Act also says it "does not affect the power of the Parliament of the United Kingdom to make laws for Scotland".
  • So the UK stays unitary: power is lent by the center, not shared by a constitution.
Quick check
?The UK created a Scottish Parliament in 1998. Why is the UK still described as a unitary state?
Mission check

?In Country Q, the national ministry in the capital appoints every regional governor, writes one school curriculum and sets one speed limit for the whole country. How would this shape the map of Country Q?

Unitary states concentrate power in one center and spread uniform rules outward. In federal states, such as the United States, power is shared, so laws like speed limits change at state lines.

Mission 8

Mission 8: Why do some countries split apart, while others hold together by handing power to their regions?

Make a guess: Why do some countries split apart, while others hold together by handing power to their regions?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • SPS-4.A define factors that lead to the devolution of states
  • SPS-4.A.1 factors include division of groups by physical geography, ethnic separatism, ethnic cleansing, terrorism, economic and social problems, and irredentism
  • SPS-4.B explain how political, economic, cultural and technological changes challenge state sovereignty (devolution part)
  • SPS-4.B.1 devolution occurs when states fragment into autonomous regions or subnational political-territorial units (Spain, Belgium, Canada, Nigeria) or when states disintegrate (Sudan, former Soviet Union)
  • SPS-4.B.2 advances in communication technology have facilitated devolution, supranationalism and democratization
Mission 8

Devolution

  • Devolution: power moves from the central government to regions inside a state.
  • Two possible outcomes:
    • Autonomy: regions gain their own governments, but the state survives.
    • Disintegration: the state breaks into separate independent states.
  • Both challenge the central government's sovereignty.
Mission 8

Factors 1: geography and separatism

  • Division by physical geography: parts of a state are far apart or cut off by seas, mountains or another country.
  • Example: the 1947 partition of India created West and East Pakistan, "two noncontiguous territories" very different in "language, ethnicity and culture"; East Pakistan seceded in 1971 to become Bangladesh.
  • Ethnic separatism: an ethnic group in one region seeks more self-rule or independence.
Mission 8

Factors 2: violence

  • Ethnic cleansing: forcibly removing an ethnic group from an area, by violence or intimidation, to make it ethnically uniform. It deepens divisions and can end in partition.
  • Terrorism: violence against civilians for political aims. Example: ETA (Euskadi Ta Askatasuna, founded 1959) used terrorism in a campaign for an independent Basque state; its violence claimed more than 800 lives before it disbanded in 2018.
Mission 8

Factors 3: grievance and claims

  • Economic and social problems: a region feels poorer, neglected, or that it pays more than its share; unemployment and inequality feed demands for self-rule. Belgium's regions were created partly because they "aspired to more economic autonomy".
  • Irredentism: a "territorial claim based on a national, ethnic, or historical basis", often by one state to land where its ethnic kin live in another state. The term comes from an Italian movement of the late 1800s and early 1900s.
Quick check
?State A claims a strip of State B's territory because many people there share State A's language and ethnicity. Which devolution factor is this?
Mission 8

Autonomy: Spain and Belgium

  • Spain: the 1978 constitution affirms "the indissoluble unity of the Spanish Nation" but "guarantees the right to self-government of the nationalities and regions of which it is composed".
  • Belgium: six state reforms between 1970 and 2014 turned it into "a federal state, composed of communities and regions".
    • Communities are based on language (Dutch, French, German).
    • Regions: Flemish, Brussels-Capital and Walloon.
Mission 8

Autonomy: Canada and Nigeria

  • Canada: the Nunavut Act created a new territory, Nunavut, with its own legislature and executive council. Quebec has its own French-speaking provincial government.
  • Nigeria: its constitution states "There shall be 36 states in Nigeria", each with its own government, sharing power in a country of many ethnic groups.
  • These are subnational political-territorial units: regions with real powers inside a state.
Quick check
?Which is an example of devolution that keeps the state together?
Mission 8

Disintegration: Sudan and the Soviet Union

  • Sudan: a 2005 peace agreement called for a referendum; in January 2011, 98.83% of participants voted for independence. South Sudan became independent on July 9, 2011 and joined the UN on July 14, 2011.
  • Soviet Union: in December 1991 leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus formed the CIS; on December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin.
  • The USSR became 15 states: the 3 Baltic states and 12 other republics.
Quick check
?In South Sudan's January 2011 referendum, 98.83% of participants voted for independence. Out of every 10,000 participants, about how many voted for independence?
Mission 8

Communication technology

  • Radio, television, the internet, mobile phones and social media let movements spread ideas, organize rallies and campaign without relying on state-controlled media.
  • Devolution: regional and separatist movements can reach supporters directly and in their own language.
  • Democratization: citizens share news and coordinate protests and elections.
  • Supranationalism: officials of many states can work together daily.
Mission check

?An invented state has an island region 500 miles from the capital. The islanders speak a different language, and a small armed group there once bombed public buildings. The central government creates an island parliament with power over schools and taxes, and the state stays united. Which description is best?

Devolution is driven by physical division, ethnic separatism, ethnic cleansing, terrorism, economic and social problems and irredentism. States respond with autonomy (Spain, Belgium, Canada, Nigeria) or break up (Sudan, the Soviet Union); communication technology makes all these movements easier to organize.

Mission 9

Mission 9: From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?

Make a guess: From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • SPS-4.B explain how political, economic, cultural and technological changes challenge state sovereignty
  • SPS-4.B.2 advances in communication technology have facilitated devolution, supranationalism and democratization
  • SPS-4.B.3 transnational and environmental challenges, economies of scale, trade agreements and military alliances further supranationalism
  • SPS-4.B.4 supranational organizations (UN, NATO, EU, ASEAN, Arctic Council, African Union) can challenge state sovereignty by limiting members' economic or political actions
Mission 9

Sovereignty and supranationalism

  • Sovereignty: a state's right to govern its own territory without outside control.
  • Supranationalism: three or more states join an organization and agree to share some powers or follow common rules.
  • Joining brings benefits, but it can limit what each member may do alone.
Mission 9

Why states join

  • Transnational and environmental problems cross borders: pollution, climate, disease, migration.
  • Economies of scale: a bigger, shared market lets firms sell more and cut costs.
  • Trade agreements lower tariffs between members.
  • Military alliances promise shared defense.
Mission 9

The European Union

  • The EU's single market ensures "free movement of goods, services, capital and persons".
  • EU law gives the Union exclusive control of the "customs union" and "common commercial policy".
  • So EU members cannot set their own tariffs or sign their own trade deals: a clear economic limit on sovereignty.
  • Free movement of persons meant members could not limit EU citizens' right to live and work there. After leaving, the UK could set its own rules for EU citizens.
Quick check
?France wants to put a tariff on imported steel from outside the EU. What happens?
Mission 9

The African Union and AfCFTA

  • AfCFTA: 44 of the 55 African Union states signed the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement in 2018; trading began on January 1, 2021. Its aim: "to eliminate trade barriers and boost intra-Africa trade".
  • African Union (AU): governments that "come to power through unconstitutional means" are not allowed to take part in its activities.
  • After a coup, the AU suspended Niger on August 22, 2023, "until the effective restoration of constitutional order": a political limit.
Mission 9

The United Nations

  • The UN has 193 member states. It "is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its Members".
  • But members "agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the Security Council".
  • The UN may not intervene in matters "essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state", except for enforcement measures, such as sanctions, ordered by the Security Council.
Mission 9

NATO: a military alliance

  • NATO has 32 member countries.
  • Article 5: "an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all".
  • NATO has invoked Article 5 only once: after the September 11, 2001 attacks on the USA.
  • Members gain shared defense but commit themselves to respond together.
Quick check
?Which organization's main purpose is collective defense?
Mission 9

ASEAN

  • The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gained its 11th member, Timor-Leste, on October 26, 2025.
  • ASEAN usually avoids interfering in members' internal affairs.
  • But after Myanmar's military took power in 2021, ASEAN leaders kept Myanmar to "non-political representation" at its summits (decision of November 2022): a limit on a member's political role.
Mission 9

The Arctic Council

  • Members: the eight Arctic states (Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, the USA).
  • Six organizations of Arctic Indigenous Peoples are Permanent Participants.
  • It tackles shared environmental issues across the region, but its mandate "explicitly excludes military security".
  • It works by cooperation, so it limits members' sovereignty far less than the EU does.
Mission 9

Communication technology

  • Supranationalism: the internet and video links let officials from many states work together every day.
  • Democratization: mobile phones and social media help citizens share news, organize and campaign.
  • Devolution: regional movements can reach supporters and the world without national media.
  • The same tools can also be used by governments to monitor and censor.
Quick check
?Which statement about supranational organizations is best supported by this mission?
Mission check

?A made-up country joins a customs union and a military alliance. How does membership change its government's control over trade and security?

Governments can shape global interactions, as the UK did by ending free movement, but supranational bodies limit what members do alone: the EU sets trade policy, the AU suspends members after coups, NATO binds members to shared defense. The answer is partly: states trade some sovereignty for benefits.

Mission 10

Mission 10: In 2023 Somalia topped the Fragile States Index. What pulls a country apart, and what holds one together?

Make a guess: In 2023 Somalia topped the Fragile States Index. What pulls a country apart, and what holds one together?

Course framework: what this mission covers

AP Human Geography

  • SPS-4.C explain how centrifugal and centripetal forces apply at the state scale
  • SPS-4.C.1 centrifugal forces may lead to failed states, uneven development, stateless nations and ethnic nationalist movements
  • SPS-4.C.2 centripetal forces can lead to ethnonationalism, more equitable infrastructure development and increased cultural cohesion
Mission 10

Forces that pull apart, forces that hold together

  • Centrifugal forces divide a state: they weaken loyalty to it or split its people.
  • Centripetal forces unify a state: they build loyalty and bind its regions together.
  • Every state has both. Its stability depends on which are stronger.
Mission 10

Failed states

  • A failed state cannot provide basic security or services, or control its own territory.
  • The Fragile States Index scores 179 countries on 12 indicators, such as security, public services and refugees.
  • 2023: Somalia ranked 1st (most fragile), then Yemen and South Sudan; Norway ranked 179th.
Mission 10

Uneven development

  • Uneven development: some regions grow richer while others are left behind.
  • Lagging regions may feel ignored by the capital; leading regions may resent paying for others. Both can pull a state apart.
  • The Fragile States Index treats "Uneven Economic Development" as one of its warning indicators.
Quick check
?Which is a centrifugal force?
Mission 10

Stateless nations

  • A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state is a territory with its own government. A stateless nation is a nation without a state of its own.
  • Example: the Kurds. Iraq's 2005 constitution recognizes "the region of Kurdistan, along with its existing authorities, as a federal region".
  • It makes Arabic and Kurdish "the two official languages of Iraq"; Kurdistan is a region within Iraq, not an independent state.
Mission 10

Ethnic nationalist movements

  • An ethnic nationalist movement seeks more self-rule, or independence, for an ethnic group inside a larger state. Kurdish self-rule in Iraq, now a recognized federal region, is one example.
  • Not every nationalist movement is ethnic. Scotland's independence movement is based on a nation of the UK, not an ethnic group. On September 18, 2014, people in Scotland voted in a referendum "to remain in the United Kingdom".
  • Such movements can use peaceful, legal votes, as in Scotland; elsewhere they have involved armed conflict.
Quick check
?Why are the Kurds an example of a stateless nation?
Mission 10

Cultural cohesion

  • Shared language, symbols and institutions build cultural cohesion.
  • Indonesia's constitution: "The national language shall be Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia)".
  • Its national motto is "Unity in Diversity (Bhinneka Tunggal Ika)": one identity across many islands and peoples.
Mission 10

Equitable infrastructure

  • Roads, rail, power and internet that reach all regions tie them to the state and to each other.
  • The US Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 expanded the Interstate system to 41,000 miles, with $25 billion authorized for 1957–1969.
  • The National Archives notes a cost too: in cities, "massive superhighways cut through neighborhoods".
Mission 10

Ethnonationalism

  • Ethnonationalism: a strong sense of nationhood tied to one ethnic group.
  • AP lists it as something centripetal forces can lead to: shared language, symbols and institutions can turn into loyalty to one ethnic nation.
  • Where most citizens share that ethnicity, this binds them to the state.
  • Where a state has several ethnic groups, the same idea can make minorities feel excluded: then it pulls apart.
Quick check
?Why can centripetal forces lead to ethnonationalism?
Mission check

?A made-up country has one region far richer than the rest, a minority people seeking independence, a national language taught in every school and a new railway linking every province. Which pair is correct?

Forces that pull apart include state failure, uneven development, stateless nations and ethnic nationalist movements. Forces that hold together include shared language and symbols and equitable infrastructure; they can also lead to ethnonationalism, which unites a state only where most citizens share one ethnicity.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • State = sovereign territory with population, government and foreign relations; nation = a people with a shared identity.
  • Types: nation-state, multinational state (UK), multistate nation (Koreans), stateless nation (Kurds), autonomous/semiautonomous regions (Native American reservations, Iraq's Kurdistan Region, Hong Kong).

Mission 2

  • Sovereignty, nation-states and self-determination shape today's map of 193 UN members.
  • Colonialism and imperialism drew many borders; independence movements made new states, often keeping colonial lines; devolution along national lines can split states.

Mission 3

  • Territoriality: people, their culture and their economies tied to land, shown by marking, mapping and defending it (Hans Island).
  • Political power = control over people, land and resources: neocolonialism (economic control of independent states), shatterbelts (divided regions between rival powers), choke points (narrow passages such as Hormuz and the Red Sea).

Mission 4

  • Boundaries are defined, delimited, demarcated and administered; they limit sovereignty, and many are contested (Eritrea–Ethiopia).
  • Types: antecedent, subsequent, consequent, superimposed, geometric, relict. Some come from policy (Berlin Conference) or ceasefires (DMZs).

Mission 5

  • Territorial sea 12 nm (sovereignty, innocent passage) · EEZ 200 nm (resource rights, free navigation) · high seas open to all · the Area common heritage.
  • Maritime boundaries and agreements can encourage interaction (Barents Sea treaty), spark resource disputes (South China Sea) and express shared identity (Pacific Islands Forum).

Mission 6

  • Voting districts are redrawn (redistricting) after each census; gerrymandering draws them for advantage using packing and cracking.
  • The effects show up at various scales: Congress, state legislatures, city councils. Checks now come mostly from state courts, laws and commissions.

Mission 7

  • Unitary: centralized, top-down, uniform rules (France). Federal: power shared with regions; dispersed power centers and a patchwork of laws (USA, Germany).
  • Unitary states can devolve powers (UK, Scotland) without becoming federal.

Mission 8

  • Six devolution factors: physical division, ethnic separatism, ethnic cleansing, terrorism, economic and social problems, irredentism.
  • Outcomes: autonomous regions / subnational units (Spain, Belgium, Canada, Nigeria) or disintegration (Sudan → South Sudan 2011; Soviet Union → 15 states 1991); communication technology aids devolution, supranationalism and democratization.

Mission 9

  • Supranational organizations (UN, NATO, EU, ASEAN, Arctic Council, AU) bring shared benefits but limit members' economic or political actions.
  • Shared problems, economies of scale, trade and defense push states together; communication technology helps.

Mission 10

  • Centrifugal forces (failed states, uneven development, stateless nations, ethnic nationalist movements) divide a state.
  • Centripetal forces unify it and can lead to cultural cohesion, more equitable infrastructure and ethnonationalism.
